issues.legal_issue: A company incorporated as a separate legal person does not become the property of the Union merely because the Union owns all its shares, so the Union’s constitutional tax immunity does not protect the company’s property.
material_facts: The appellant was a company incorporated under the Companies Act, and its shares were wholly owned by the Union.
The company was assessed in respect of land that it used, although the land itself was owned by the Central Government.
issues.conclusion: Article 285 did not apply to the company’s property or prevent assessment against it; the company remained a legal entity distinct from the Union.
issues.legal_principle: Article 285 exempts the property of the Union from State taxation, but does not make a company’s property Union property merely because the Union holds its shares. The Court relied on Western Coalfields Limited v. Special Area Development Authority, Korba, Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India, and Heavy Engineering Mazdoor Union v. State of Bihar, which recognize the separate legal personality of an incorporated company and distinguish company property from shareholder property. The Court also referred to New Delhi Municipal Council v. State of Punjab for the absolute character of Article 285’s protection, but held it inapplicable where the property being assessed was not the Union’s property.

rule.if: constitutional_tax_immunity_claim and incorporated_company and government_owns_company_shares and company_has_separate_legal_personality

predicates.constitutional_tax_immunity_claim: A party in a tax dispute claims that constitutional immunity for Union property prevents the assessment.
predicates.incorporated_company: The entity whose property or liability is at issue was incorporated as a company.
predicates.government_owns_company_shares: The Union owns all or some of the company’s shares.
predicates.company_has_separate_legal_personality: The company exists as a legal person distinct from its shareholders.

issues.definition: When a tax-immunity claim concerns an incorporated company with separate legal personality, government ownership of its shares does not make the company’s property immune as Union property.

issues.legal_issue: A lessee of government-owned land leased for a non-agricultural purpose is liable for assessment when the governing law treats that lessee as the owner.
material_facts: The Central Government owned the land and had leased it to the appellant company for industrial and commercial use.
The amended law included a lessee of government land leased for a commercial, industrial, or other non-agricultural purpose within the definition of owner.
The company challenged demands for non-agricultural assessment on the land.
issues.conclusion: For periods to which the amendment applied, the company was treated as the owner and was liable for assessment on the qualifying leased land.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(j) and 3 of the Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, 1963, as amended, treated a lessee of government land leased for a commercial, industrial, or other non-agricultural purpose as an owner liable to pay assessment. Section 12, as amended, brought such leased government land within the Act. The Court also applied the principle that a company is a separate legal entity from its government shareholder, relying on Western Coalfields Limited v. Special Area Development Authority, Korba, Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India, and Heavy Engineering Mazdoor Union v. State of Bihar.

rule.if: assessment_challenge and government_owned_land_leased_to_company and lease_for_non_agricultural_purpose and law_treats_lessee_as_owner

predicates.assessment_challenge: A company challenges an assessment imposed on land it occupies under a lease.
predicates.government_owned_land_leased_to_company: The land is owned by a government and has been leased to the company.
predicates.lease_for_non_agricultural_purpose: The land was leased for a commercial, industrial, or other non-agricultural purpose.
predicates.law_treats_lessee_as_owner: The applicable law treats a lessee of such government land as an owner liable for assessment.

issues.definition: A company that challenges an assessment is liable as the statutory owner where it leases government land for a non-agricultural purpose and the applicable law assigns liability to the lessee.

issues.legal_issue: An amendment imposing assessment liability cannot support demands for periods before the amendment took effect when the liability claim rests on that amendment.
material_facts: The demands included periods before and after the 1974 amendment took effect.
The State’s defence to the company’s challenge rested on the amendments made in 1974.
The amendments had no retrospective effect.
issues.conclusion: Demands for periods before the amendment took effect were quashed.
issues.legal_principle: The amendments made by Act 28 of 1974 to the definition of owner and the scope of the Act had no retrospective effect. They could not support an assessment demand for a period before they came into force.

predicates.assessment_demand_challenge: A party challenges a demand for assessment imposed on land.
predicates.liability_claimed_under_amendment: The asserted liability depends on a statutory amendment.
predicates.demand_period_precedes_amendment: The demand covers a period before the amendment took effect.

issues.definition: A demand for a period before an amendment took effect is invalid when the asserted assessment liability depends on that amendment.

issues.legal_issue: Assessment on leased land covered by the Act is confined to the land actually used for a specified non-agricultural purpose, and the extent and applicable rate may be determined on appeal.
material_facts: The company claimed that only some portions of the land were used for buildings, roads, or other purposes, while some land was reserved for future expansion or used for agriculture.
The High Court left the actual extent of qualifying land and the applicable rate to be determined by the statutory appellate authority.
The Supreme Court allowed the companies to appeal on those matters and stated that assessment could be levied only on qualifying land.
issues.conclusion: Assessment could be levied only on the extent actually used for commercial, industrial, or other non-agricultural purposes; the companies could appeal to establish that extent and contest the applicable rate.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(j), 3, and 12 of the Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, 1963, as amended, apply to the relevant leased government land and impose assessment liability on the statutory owner. The assessment is limited to land actually used for the specified commercial, industrial, or other non-agricultural purposes. The actual extent and applicable rate may be canvassed before and decided by the statutory appellate authority.

predicates.assessment_appeal: A party appeals a demand for assessment on leased land.
predicates.leased_land_contains_areas_not_used_for_: Some of the leased land was not actually used for commercial, industrial, or other non-agricultural purposes.

issues.definition: On appeal, assessment is confined to the leased land actually used for qualifying purposes, and the appellate authority may determine the extent and rate.

issues.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel does not prevent assessment contrary to a statute, and a statement that no separate exemption notification is required for government-run public-sector units does not promise exemption to a separate company.
material_facts: A government letter stated that no separate notification was required to exempt the land from assessment so long as the units were run by the Union in the public sector.
The appellant was a company with a legal identity separate from the Union and ran its own industry.
The company claimed that it had acted on the letter and that the State was estopped from assessing it.
issues.conclusion: The State was not estopped from assessing the company: estoppel could not operate against the statute, and the letter did not promise an exemption to a separate company.
issues.legal_principle: There can be no estoppel against a statute. In addition, the letter, read according to its terms, did not promise exemption to a company that was a separate legal entity and ran its own industry. The Court applied the separate-entity principle recognized in Western Coalfields Limited v. Special Area Development Authority, Korba, Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India, and Heavy Engineering Mazdoor Union v. State of Bihar.

predicates.promissory_estoppel_claim_in_assessment_: A company claims that a government promise prevents an assessment imposed on it.
predicates.statute_imposes_assessment_liability: The applicable statute imposes assessment liability on the company in the circumstances.
predicates.communication_does_not_promise_company_e: The government communication does not promise an exemption to the company itself.
predicates.company_is_separate_from_government: The company has a legal identity distinct from the government.

issues.definition: A company cannot use a government communication to prevent assessment where the statute imposes liability, the communication does not promise that company an exemption, and the company is legally separate from the government.

issues.legal_issue: A party may not advance on appeal a contention that contradicts the position it took in its original pleading.
material_facts: In its writ petition, the company asserted that it was the lessee of the government-owned land.
On appeal, counsel argued that the company was not a lessee and that no lease existed in its favour.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the contention because it contradicted the company’s case in its writ petition.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated a submission contrary to the party’s own pleaded case as impermissible and declined to consider it.

predicates.appeal_from_challenged_demand: A party appeals in a proceeding concerning a challenged assessment demand.
predicates.appellate_argument_contradicts_original_: The party advances an appellate contention that contradicts its position in its original pleading.

issues.definition: In an appeal concerning a challenged demand, the court may decline to consider a contention that contradicts the party’s original pleading.
